results.text:
# What are you actually choosing together?

A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? It conjures up for me thoughts of romance, sex, exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, spiritual partnership, family identity, or just “we really like each other and we’ll see.” Lack of specificity is sometimes a nice way to flow, but the problem is that each person could be imagining a different bundle from those pieces, then either not labeling anything or assuming one relationship label settled it.

Before you commit to one type of relationship, ask each other: What are we deciding to join together, and why?

One honest option is basically a "practical partnership." This is very common, especially outside the modern West. Two people may share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, and maybe have sex, without pretending the whole thing rests on overwhelming romantic love.

Although this feels wrong to me and anyone else who has been in love, arguably, there is nothing inherently wrong with it if both people know that’s what they are doing. Practical motives can coexist with real affection. My objection is more personal: being valued for a role can feel good and still leave me lonely if I don't also feel held as a person.

This arrangement has been promoted throughout history because its practical obligations aren't based on highly fluctuating feelings. But that stability belongs to the duties, not necessarily to everything the people will feel. Romantic longing can still make the arrangement unstable. Imagine you’re in this, and then one day you find your heartthrob at work or church or somewhere else, and suddenly you wonder why you ever settled for less.

That vulnerability is not only a question for a practical partnership. And the biggie, whatever the arrangement: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? What counts as betrayal, and what just means we need a serious conversation?

For people who also want romance, another honest option is a romance with humility, even if romance and humility seem to clash. Two people really are in love, really do want to build something together, and really do take the bond seriously, but they do not pretend they can guarantee the feeling forever.

They can still choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life. The honest part is that they admit feelings can change, and they talk beforehand about what that would mean. If the romance fades, maybe they revive it, or maybe they renegotiate the arrangement.

Is this mainly a romance, a practical partnership, or both? Are we promising actions, or quietly pretending to promise permanent feelings? If the romance changes, which parts of this agreement still remain?

Which needs should still be supported mostly outside the relationship?

My actual ideal is to have intimacy embedded in community.

Obviously most people are not going to live in a free-love community unless we really have a New Earth soon. But, as Pema Chodron says to prisoners when teaching them meditation, "Start Where You Are." Build mutual friendships, and keep other sources of meaning and support alive.

How should we plan on revisiting this agreement when our lives change?

If we separate, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe any children involved?

These are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with! You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there's real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity.
